results.title: Low Bandwidth Strategies | Training For Change
results.content: As facilitators, we can’t control participants’ internet access, but we can use strategies to support connection and learning regardless of bandwidth. Supporting low-bandwidth participants increases accessibility overall. These strategies also support people who are new or have limited access to technology, low literacy, and/or with visual impairment. When inviting participants to engage using higher tech tools, provide low-bandwidth options too. This helps you know whether every type of connection is being engaged and who might need extra support. * Invite the group to track with you using participation formats like “choose who is next,” where you ask one person to share on a topic, then they choose someone else who hasn’t shared and so on until everyone has spoken. When you have a low tech connection to a meeting (like being on the phone only) or are having problems (like your internet cutting out) it can feel like you are on the margins of the group looking in. * Verbalize what you are tracking about the group’s participation. #### Use low bandwidth visuals/tools. * The facilitator and one other person can scribe while the group shares in chat or out loud only. Using the time before and after your group gets together can help maximize the engagement for your participants. These “asynchronous” strategies include preparing for those who you know will have low bandwidth and also helping those who unexpectedly had intermittent access to the call. This can especially help those who may have bandwidth or tech access intermittently and also supports participants who need more time or quiet to process and think. * Check in with your group ahead of time to find out how people will be connecting and to share options and support. * Check in afterwards with group members who had low connectivity. When leading a group with low-bandwidth participants, it’s helpful to have a team member who can pay attention to specific individuals who might be having trouble. * While one person facilitates, the other can offer more individualized support to people whose call is dropping constantly, or who are having trouble getting the information being shared.

results.title: How to Optimize UX for Low Bandwidth and Poor Connectivity Users
results.content:
Title: How to Optimize UX for Low Bandwidth and Poor Connectivity Users
# How to Optimize UX for Low Bandwidth and Poor Connectivity Users. Low bandwidth and poor internet connectivity are part of everyday life for millions of users now that the internet and digital technologies have become essential. Optimizing user experience for them is necessary, but it becomes a necessity in order to allow inclusiveness and accessibility. In this article, we shall discuss and explore the best practices and strategies to enhance the user experience of those users with connectivity issues. The first step towards designing a better experience is to understand the needs of such users. ## Critical Principles of UX Optimization for Low Connectivity. When designing an application, everything should be simple, especially when considering low-bandwidth users. An onslaught of too many elements on the interface slows down loading times and seems to confuse the user. Making your design accessible ensures that every user can interact with your content. Accessible design is fundamentally about creating a positive user experience for everyone. **Use Lazy Loading:** In this technique, images and videos load only when they enter the user's viewport, which tends to reduce load time hugely at the primary stage. Users returning to a site more than once can have pages loaded faster because their browser fetches information locally rather than having it fetched from the server each time. Using progressive enhancement provides the flexibility to correct the most critical content for low-bandwidth users first. You may start with an application that loads quickly and adds more advanced features for better connection users. This will ensure that every user still has access to a working experience, no matter how bad their connection is. Conduct a usability test with actual users in a low-bandwidth environment. Collect feedback from users who now understand pain points and will thus improve your design upon receiving that feedback. Many brands have successfully optimized UX for low-bandwidth environments. Low-bandwidth and low-connectivity users are very important in a wider, inclusive digital environment, so optimizing UX is worth it. By keeping it simple, using content delivery strategies, and continuing to test and refine your approach, you'll ensure that all users have a smooth journey.

results.title: Designing for Users with Low Digital Literacy: UI/UX Tips
results.content: # UI/UX Tips: Designing for Users with Low Digital Literacy. By creating interfaces that are intuitive, clear, and frustration-free, we can help users with low digital literacy confidently interact with technology. * **Equitable Use:** Your design should work just as well for a digital newbie as for a seasoned user. * **Flexibility in Use:** Allow users to customize settings like font size, color contrast, and language. UI/UX Best Practices for Low Digital Literacy Users**. * **User Research:** Involve low digital literacy users right from the start. ### Designing for Evolving User Needs. * **Young and Transitional Users:** As digital literacy continues to grow among younger populations, interfaces will need to offer both simplicity for beginners and depth for those who are ready to explore advanced features. * **Longitudinal Studies:** Track how users’ digital literacy improves over time with iterative design changes. With continuous testing and iterative improvements, our designs can evolve alongside our users, making the digital world less intimidating and more inviting.
